title: Ben wanted to work a grill like SpongeBob, so we built him a whole food court he can run with a single switch
author: acrolicious
selftext:
This is my brother Ben. He has a rare condition that slowly took his voice and his mobility, and along with them, his ability to play games. Recently he told us he wanted a game where he could run a kitchen and manage food like a fry cook, kind of like SpongeBob at the Krusty Krab. Ben has never had a job before, so we wanted to give him that experience in a way that's fun, and that turned into Ben's Food Court, a simulation game with a bunch of different food service jobs he can jump into, starting with the burger grill.

Games like this don't really exist for someone like Ben, who plays independently with one or two buttons. So over time we've been building a whole library of switch-accessible games and tools on Benny's Hub and SwitchedGames, where you can use a single button to get to everything, from the menus to the games themselves. We build mostly with Claude in VS Code, and we keep using AI to make new experiences for him and for anyone else who plays this way. It's kind of wild to me that none of this existed before, and I have to give AI a lot of credit for helping us make it possible.

What we're building isn't groundbreaking in the traditional sense, but it's for a community of people who have been left out of gaming for a long time. Everything we make is free and open source, and we share our game dev guide too, because we think it's so important that others can easily access these games and make their own. We know the pain of watching Ben lose the ability to play, so we want to give back as much as we can to help families like ours.

We love sharing on Reddit and social media because we're hoping to reach other families who have been waiting for games like these, and to show them they can use AI to make games too if they want to. Our nonprofit, NARBE Foundation, also donates free switch kits to families like ours.

I'll put all the links in the comments. Thank you for checking it out and sharing it. You never know who it might reach and help.

comments.author: acrolicious
comments.body:
Links for anyone who wants to check it out or build their own:


- Ben's Food Court: https://narbehouse.github.io/bens-food-court/
- Benny's Hub: https://bennyshub.com
- SwitchedGames library: https://switchedgames.org
- Free switch kits for families: https://narbefoundation.org
- Our game dev guides: https://narbehouse.github.io/

Everything is free and open source, so feel free to use it, remix it, or reach out if you want help getting started.

comments.author: horsewitnoname
comments.body: Wait this is really cool and such a good cause. How does a switch like this work in a game? Is eye-tracking involved?

replies.author: acrolicious
replies.body:
No eye tracking. (It could be used,  I guess) Ben's condition causes nystagmus and eye tracking doesn't work - the two buttons on his head are his best method for access. (No, Neuralink isn't an option for us and Ben doesn't have enough control of his mouth or other access methods people always suggest - he can uses these buttons and it's the best we've found)

It's simply scan and select options. 

You can use everything with spacebar and return or just return if you have auto scan turned on. 

Check out https://www.switchedgames.org to see how it works 😊

replies.author: horsewitnoname
replies.body:
Oh wow I completely missed the big buttons on the side of his head! Thought it was a medical device at first! This is really amazing, I think I really want my next project to be something like this.
Thanks for sharing!

comments.author: caesium23
comments.body: For one of the games I'm working on, I've tried to keep everything tab-accessible following browser standards. Is that pretty much what Ben needs to be able to play?

replies.author: acrolicious
replies.body:
Thanks for thinking about this! Tab is a great start, but Ben uses head switches that send Space and Enter, which are pretty standard for switch access. What he needs is built-in scanning: Space moves a highlight between options and Enter selects (or with one switch, it auto-scans and a press selects). Big highlights, spoken options, and no fast timing or button holds help too.

We have a guide for this, and everything is open source, including our accessibility MD files, so anyone can use them to build switch-accessible games like ours. You can find it all at https://narbehouse.github.io/developer-guide.html

replies.author: caesium23
replies.body: I'll look at the guide. I'm curious though, any idea why these switches standardized on space+enter when the entire web standardized on tab+enter?

replies.author: acrolicious
replies.body:
Not entirely sure but Space and Enter are the most common defaults on switch interfaces and in switch software, including the Windows On-Screen Keyboard's scanning mode. Many interfaces can also send Tab, so Tab + Enter can work, it just isn't the usual default.

For Ben specifically, tabbing through a website isn't something he's ever done. He's never used a computer that way. We built his interface and the whole ecosystem around Space and Enter scanning because that's the accessibility standard for switch users.

replies.author: caesium23
replies.body:
Hmm, from a brief search, it looks like web accessibility standards are really oriented around keyboards and actually assumes more than just two buttons are available – tab+enter are the backbone, and thus the ones I'm most familiar with, but technically space and arrow keys are in the mix too.

Switch compatibility at two buttons, or even just one, is even more limited. The good news is it's the same basic concept as tab-accessibility, so if you have one you're already most of the way to being able to support the other, but the expected behaviors are just different enough that they will need to be separate modes or input profiles. I'll have to make a note of that for when I get to that point with my next game.

My first game was [Orbit Shift](https://playgama.com/game/orbit-shift?clid=p_378af4bf-f2b1-4559-8d65-6e8fa32c90c6), which is basically a one-tap infinite runner in space. I see in your guidelines anything based on reaction time and precision may just be a no-go, but if you think Ben would be interested in playing something like this if it could be adapted to his needs, let me know and I'll see what I can do. It would be easy to add a slower mode.

comments.body: So amazing! I hope he gets a Bikini Bottom / Krusty Krab version sometime
